title: How a fly knows which way it's facing
summary: Push a real fly's compass around and see what holds it in place.

steps.text: Tap Stimulate to fire the left turn neurons (the turning signal). Then watch the compass dial.
steps.result: The compass neurons (the heading cells) light up on one side. That bright patch, the bump, marks which way the fly faces.

steps.text: Now tap Stimulate on the right turn neurons (the other signal). Keep your eyes on the bump.
steps.result: The bump swung around the dial. Turning signals from each side push it opposite ways, so the fly's heading turns too.

steps.text: Silence the ring neurons (the landmark carriers). They bring in what the fly sees. We will send the right signal for you.
steps.result: The bump slips off its spot and wanders. Without landmarks, the compass drifts.

steps.text: Tap the ring neurons (the landmark carriers) button again to switch them back on. We will send the same signal.
steps.result: The bump holds its spot again. Landmarks keep the fly's compass true.

check.question: You silenced the landmark carriers (the violet cells). Why did the bump drift?

choices.text: The turning signal never reached the compass.
choices.feedback: Not quite. The green heading cells still lit up, so the signal got there. Nothing held the bump in place.

choices.text: Nothing told the compass where the landmarks were, so the bump slid.
choices.feedback: Yes! The violet cells bring in what the fly sees. Without them, nothing pins the bump to the world.

choices.text: You switched off the green heading cells too.
choices.feedback: Not quite. You only silenced the violet cells. The green heading cells kept firing, but nothing held them still.

freePlay.title: Free play
freePlay.text: Every button works now. Guess first, then tap: where does the bump go if you fire both turning signals at once? Try it with the violet cells silenced.
